newsitem.title: MEXICO: Biggest explosion in 70 years at Mexican volcano.
newsitem.headline: Biggest explosion in 70 years at Mexican volcano.

text.p: Tens of thousands of people were on emergency alert on Tuesday after a giant volcano near Mexico City belched red-hot rocks and giant clouds of ash in its biggest eruption in 72 years.

Clouds of ash and acrid gases showered down on much of Mexico City late on Monday from the snow-capped 17,890-foot (5,452 metre) Popocatepetl volcano, forcing a temporary closure of the international airport. Popocatepetl is 33 miles (50 km) southeast of the capital.

Disaster prevention officials said on Tuesday activity in the volcano appeared to be subsiding and one runway of the airport was reopened, but television showed Popocatepetl blowing out another gray mushroom cloud early in the day.
"The (volcano tracking) system will remain in the same state of alert as yesterday," Puebla state Gov. Manuel Bartlett told Televisa on the breakfast news program.

Troops and emergency personnel were rushed to 30 farming villages at the foot of Popocatepetl in preparation for an evacuation. Inhabitants said they were reluctant to leave their homes for fear their possessions would be stolen.

Winds blew the fine gray dirt as far east as the Caribbean port of Veracruz and residents complained of burning eyes and throats. No injuries were reported in the eruption, the most intense of several this year.
"It feels like sand. It gets into your throat and your teeth. We've never seen anything like this," Maria del Carmen Ariaga said as she watched the blanket of ash fall.

Puebla, an industrial city of around one million, is about 38 miles (60 km) east of the volcano, which straddles the states of Puebla and Mexico. An official from the National Commission for the Prevention of Disasters told radio network Radio Red on Tuesday that at least 193,000 people were earmarked for evacuation from Puebla alone. He gave no figure for Mexico, a heavily populated state surrounding Mexico City.
Anxious to avoid panic, authorities played down Monday's explosion despite the red alert, which has hundreds of troops and dozens of vehicles in place for an emergency evacuation.
"The situation is calm. We are practically in a normal situation," Bartlett said.

Monday's eruption started at 5.55 p.m. (2255 GMT) and lasted for 35 minutes, during which burning rocks pounded down the volcano's sides, threatening nearby villages. Authorities initially urged Mexico City's 18 million residents to stay indoors and close doors and windows. Those who needed to go outside were advised to wear goggles and face masks.

Mexico City drivers, forced to get out to wipe their windshields repeatedly, were stuck in traffic jams for hours. Confusion was compounded on Monday evening as the federal government first declared, then denied a red alert.

"There was confusion. There never was a red alert," Ricardo Garcia Villalobos, undersecretary for civil protection at the Interior Ministry, told a news conference. Civil defense officials had earlier declared a red alert.
Interior Minister Emilio Chauyffet said authorities were standing by to evacuate people if the volcano grew volatile again but he said its activity had dropped notably.
Experts said "Popo," as the mountain is affectionately known, had registered its most violent activity since 1925.

The volcano, whose name means "smoking mountain" in the local Nahuatl Indian language, has blown out ash and steam on numerous occasions this year. But Monday's explosion was the first time the grit-like ash had rained down on Mexico City.
